# Hill Climbing an LLM Judge on TPR and TNR: A Worked Example With an Answer Key

Bryan Falkowski · October 2026 · Code and data: [github.com/bfalkowski/judge-tpr-tnr](https://github.com/bfalkowski/judge-tpr-tnr)

*Draft. Every number is generated by scripts in the repo from runs on its `data` branch; `paper/results.md` and `paper/climb_table.md` hold the tables.*

**Abstract.** A common way to build an LLM judge is to label a set of traces, split them into train, dev and test, refine the judge on dev until its true positive rate (TPR) and true negative rate (TNR) pass a target, run it once on test, and then use TPR and TNR to correct the pass rate it reports on new traces. In most write-ups the labels are one person's judgment, so the reader cannot see whether each step really helped or whether the corrected pass rate is right. I ran the whole procedure on a support-agent eval where the labels come from code: the support policy is a function, so every trace has a known correct answer. I started from the judge in my previous paper, which passed 5 of every 6 real agent mistakes.

Four steps on dev took the judge from TPR 0.84 and TNR 0.52 to TPR 0.95 and TNR 0.97: precise Pass/Fail definitions, few-shot examples, and then a different, stronger model than the agent's. On a held-out test set the frozen judge scored TPR 0.93 and TNR 0.92. I then used it to estimate the pass rate of four new agent runs and compared each estimate with the truth. The judge's raw pass rate was within 1.5 points of the truth on every run. The corrected estimate was off by 2.2 to 3.3 points, although its 95% interval contained the truth every time. The reason is that the correction assumes the judge makes mistakes on new data at the rates measured on test. The answer key shows that assumption failing for weaker judges: the original judge's TNR ranged from 0.19 to 0.67 across the four runs, against 0.53 on test, because which mistakes it misses depends on which mistakes the agent makes. The whole study cost about $2.35 in API calls.

**In practice:** hill climb the judge first, then correct. Measure TPR and TNR on failures the system actually produces, not on wrong answers you constructed. Report the corrected pass rate with its interval, and check that the judge's error rates hold on fresh labels before trusting the point estimate.

## 1. The problem

In [my previous paper](https://bfalkowski.github.io/writing/run-valid.html), a judge asked whether a support agent's resolution followed the policy. Asked twice about the same item, it gave the same answer 96.5% of the time. Compared with a deterministic check, its first answer was wrong on 24.5% of items. A judge can be consistent and still be wrong, and asking it twice does not tell you which.

The fix is to compare the judge against labels it has not seen. That comparison has a standard form, taught in Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar's course AI Evaluation for Engineers and PMs and published in Husain's [guide to LLM-as-a-judge](https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/llm-judge/) and their [`validate-evaluator` skill](https://github.com/ai-evals-course/evals-skills). This paper runs that procedure from start to finish on one judge, with an answer key, so each step can be checked.

This is a worked example, not a recommendation to judge this task with an LLM. A rule that can be written as code should be checked by code, which is why paper 2 used a deterministic scorer. Here the policy stands in for a criterion that would normally need a person's judgment. The procedure is the same either way. The answer key only makes it checkable.

## 2. The method

### 2.1 TPR and TNR

The judge gives each item a verdict, PASS or FAIL. The label gives the right answer. Every item lands in one of four cells:

| | Judge PASS | Judge FAIL |
|---|---|---|
| **Labeled PASS** | true positive (TP) | false negative (FN) |
| **Labeled FAIL** | false positive (FP) | true negative (TN) |

- **TPR = TP / (TP + FN).** Of the items that should pass, the share the judge passes.
- **TNR = TN / (TN + FP).** Of the items that should fail, the share the judge fails.

These are the sensitivity and specificity of a diagnostic test (Altman and Bland 1994), with PASS as the positive class. They are kept separate because each moves the judge's reported pass rate in a different direction. A judge that misses real passes (low TPR) reports a pass rate that is too low. A judge that passes real failures (low TNR) reports one that is too high. A single accuracy number hides which is happening, and when failures are rare it can look high while the judge misses most of them.

### 2.2 Splits

Labeled items are split into three disjoint sets. Train (10 to 20%) is a pool of few-shot examples for the judge's prompt. Dev (40 to 45%) is where the judge is refined. Test (40 to 45%) is used once, after the judge is frozen. Dev and test should each hold roughly 30 to 50 items of each label, even if that over-represents failures. These figures follow Husain's guide and the `validate-evaluator` skill. Items from dev and test must never appear in the prompt.

### 2.3 The loop

1. Write a judge prompt.
2. Run it on dev. Compute TPR and TNR.
3. Read the disagreements: false passes and false fails.
4. Change one thing based on what you read: the definitions, the examples, the model, or how the criterion is split up.
5. Repeat until TPR and TNR both pass a target. The `validate-evaluator` skill uses 0.9, with 0.8 as a floor.
6. Freeze the judge. Run it once on test. The test TPR and TNR are the ones you report.

Shankar et al. (2024) show why the loop includes reading: grading outputs changes what people think the criterion is. Reading the judge's disagreements is also how label problems come to light.

### 2.4 Correcting the pass rate

A judge with known TPR and TNR can estimate the true pass rate θ of new, unlabeled traces. If the judge passes k of m traces, the observed rate is p_obs = k / m, and (Rogan and Gladen 1978):

θ̂ = (p_obs + TNR − 1) / (TPR + TNR − 1), clipped to [0, 1].

The denominator, TPR + TNR − 1, is Youden's J (Youden 1950). It is 1 for a perfect judge and 0 for a judge no better than chance. Every error in p_obs, TPR or TNR is divided by it, so a weak judge turns small errors into large ones.

A 95% interval comes from the bootstrap (Efron and Tibshirani 1993): resample, recompute TPR, TNR and θ̂, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. The reference implementation, [judgy](https://github.com/ai-evals-course/judgy), resamples test items and holds p_obs fixed. In this study items come in clusters, several per ticket, so I resample tickets instead (Field and Welsh 2007), on both the test set and the new run. Section 9.4 shows why that matters.

The correction rests on one assumption: the judge makes mistakes on the new traces at the rates measured on test.

## 3. Setup

**The agent.** Paper 2's support agent, imported unchanged from [eval-run-validity](https://github.com/bfalkowski/eval-run-validity) at commit `12a0eef`. For each ticket it looks up the order and stock and asks Jev, a small decision model from TypeSafe, which of four actions the five-rule support policy calls for: refund, reship, escalate, or reply only. I ran it under four of paper 2's configurations, so the agent makes different mixes of mistakes:

| Config | What changes |
|---|---|
| clean | nothing |
| template_edit | decision instructions become "Pick the action that best keeps this customer happy." |
| context_strip | stock levels removed from the agent's context |
| prompt_edit | the older policy without the $500 refund limit |

**The answer key.** Paper 2's reference policy function, unchanged. An item is PASS when the agent's action is the one the function returns for that ticket, order and stock. The judge always sees the true policy, order and stock, whatever the agent saw.

**Tickets.** v2 is paper 2's 60 hand-written tickets, each hard in one deliberate way. On v2, paper 2's agent made only 28 distinct mistakes across all 73 of its usable runs. The agent repeats itself, so rerunning it adds little. The method needs 30 to 50 failures in each of dev and test, so I generated more tickets in two steps, following the dimensions-then-text approach in the evals-skills `generate-synthetic-data` skill. First the facts: issue, order status, days since delivery or shipping weighted toward the 14- and 30-day cutoffs, order totals weighted toward the $500 limit, and stock. Then the text: a customer framing (plain, demand, wrong claim, angry, or indirect) rendered from phrase banks. v3 has 240 tickets. v4 has 200 more and is used only in Section 8.

**Labeled data.** The agent made 5,340 decisions on v2 and v3: 4,380 from paper 2's runs on v2 and 960 from new runs on v3, four configs times 240 tickets, for $0.03. The judge's input is fully determined by the ticket, order, stock and action, so I keep one item per distinct (ticket, action): 402 items, every one a decision the agent actually made.

| Split | Tickets | Items | PASS | FAIL | Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| train | 60 (v2) | 86 | 58 | 28 | few-shot examples only |
| dev | 120 (v3) | 158 | 87 | 71 | refining the judge |
| test | 120 (v3) | 158 | 96 | 62 | one run of the frozen judge |

Splits are by ticket, so no ticket has items in two splits. v2 is train because it had already been studied closely in paper 2. v3 is split 50/50 within each combination of framing and whether the agent ever failed the ticket. Code refuses to run any judge on test except the one recorded as frozen.

**Runs.** Every judge and agent run executed in GitHub Actions and is committed to the repo's `data` branch with a manifest: the judge's fingerprint (a hash of its prompt, examples and model), the model, the commit, and the spend. On dev and test each judge was called twice per item; on v4, once. Results use the first call. Section 6 reports how often the two calls disagreed.

## 4. The baseline and its errors

The starting judge is paper 2's, verbatim: Jev, given the policy, the ticket, the order, the stock and the agent's action, asked one question, "Does the agent's resolution follow the support policy for this ticket and order?" Jev returns a score from 0 to 1; a score of 0.5 or more is PASS.

On dev it scored TPR 0.84 and TNR 0.52. It passed 34 of the agent's 71 wrong decisions. Grouping its 48 errors by the rule that decides each item showed two problems:

- **Counting days at a cutoff (35 errors).** It passed refunds on orders delivered 31 or more days ago, where the policy requires escalation (12). It passed refunds and reships on orders shipped 14 days ago or less, where the only correct action is a reply (17). It failed correct replies and escalations on the same kinds of orders (6).
- **The $500 limit when out of stock (5 errors).** An order that is lost or overdue and cannot be reshipped is refunded, but a refund over $500 must be escalated. It passed the refunds.

The errors were not concentrated in tickets where the customer pushes for an action or misstates the facts: 23 of the 48 came from those tickets, which make up 84 of the 158 dev items.

## 5. The climb on dev

Each step changed one thing, chosen from the previous step's errors.

| Step | Change | Model | TPR [95% CI] | TNR [95% CI] | False passes | False fails |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Paper 2's judge, one sentence | Jev | 0.84 [0.76, 0.91] | 0.52 [0.42, 0.62] | 34 | 14 |
| 1 | Precise Pass/Fail definitions | Jev | 0.94 [0.89, 0.99] | 0.73 [0.62, 0.83] | 19 | 5 |
| 2 | Four train examples with critiques | Jev | 0.91 [0.84, 0.96] | 0.82 [0.72, 0.90] | 13 | 8 |
| 3 | Same prompt on Claude Haiku 4.5, reasoning then answer | Claude | 0.95 [0.91, 0.99] | 0.97 [0.93, 1.00] | 2 | 4 |

Intervals resample tickets. Each step cost about a cent on Jev; step 3 cost $0.57.

**Step 1: definitions.** The prompt now says what PASS and FAIL mean and how to decide. Use the order record, not the customer's account. Count the days from today to the delivery or shipping date before applying a cutoff. The customer's requested action never changes the required one. The $500 limit applies to refunds only. Both rates rose. All 19 remaining false passes were still at the day cutoffs.

**Step 2: examples.** Four items from train, one on each side of each cutoff, each with a short critique that shows the day count, for example: "Shipped 2026-09-17, today is 2026-10-01: 14 days, not delivered. 14 days or less is too early, so the only correct action is reply." TNR rose to 0.82 and TPR fell to 0.91, a trade the error table makes visible. Nine of the 13 false passes were still the 14-day cutoff, even with a worked example of exactly that case.

**Step 3: a different model.** When prompting stops helping, the method suggests a more capable model. The agent here is also Jev, and a judge on the agent's own model may share its blind spots (Section 9.2). Step 3 keeps step 2's definitions and examples and moves them to Claude Haiku 4.5, pinned to the dated model ID `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` so a provider update cannot change the judge silently. Claude returns a short reasoning that states the dates and day count, then "Pass" or "Fail". Both rates passed 0.9.

**Stopping.** After step 3 there were six dev errors, two each of three kinds:

- Two refunds of exactly $500, which the policy allows (the limit is "over $500"). The judge treated $500 as over the limit.
- Two escalations on orders the customer says never came but the record shows delivered. The judge applied the wrong rule.
- Two replies to damage reported on an order the record shows as shipped but not delivered. This is a label question, not just a judge error. The policy's damage rule covers delivered orders only, so the answer key says reply. The judge, told to trust the order record, applied the not-arrived rule instead: shipped more than 14 days ago and not delivered, so reship or refund. The policy text does not settle it.

I stopped there. Both rates were past the target, and a fix for two dev items is a fix fitted to dev. Before running test, I recorded two decisions in the repo (`paper/decisions.md`). The frozen judge is step 3. The labels stay as they are: the answer key was fixed before any judge was built, and changing it after reading the judge's disagreements would move the key toward the judge. Instead, test results are reported with and without the damage-on-undelivered items.

## 6. Test

| Split | Items | TP | FN | FP | TN | TPR | TNR | TPR + TNR − 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| dev | 158 | 83 | 4 | 2 | 69 | 0.954 | 0.972 | 0.926 |
| test | 158 | 89 | 7 | 5 | 57 | 0.927 | 0.919 | 0.846 |
| test without the pre-declared ambiguous items | 146 | 87 | 1 | 3 | 55 | 0.989 | 0.948 | 0.937 |

The frozen judge passed 0.9 on both rates on test, a few points below dev, as expected for a judge tuned on dev. Eight of its 12 test errors are damage or a wrong item reported on an order not yet delivered, the category flagged before the run. The other four are customers who say an order never came when the record shows it delivered. Its two calls per item never disagreed (0 of 158). The test run cost $0.58.

## 7. The calculation, start to finish

This uses the frozen judge's test rates and a fresh agent run it has never seen.

**Step 1: measure the judge on labeled data.** From the test table: TPR = 89 / 96 = 0.927 and TNR = 57 / 62 = 0.919.

**Step 2: run the judge on new traces.** v4 is 200 new tickets, in no split, never seen by any version of the judge. The agent's clean run on v4 made m = 200 decisions. The frozen judge, scoring them without labels, passed k = 152. So p_obs = 152 / 200 = 0.760.

**Step 3: correct.**

θ̂ = (0.760 + 0.919 − 1) / (0.927 + 0.919 − 1) = 0.679 / 0.846 = **0.803**

**Step 4: put an interval on it.** Resampling test tickets and v4 tickets 10,000 times gives a 95% interval of **[0.724, 0.888]**.

**Step 5: check against the answer key.** The true pass rate of the run is **0.770**, inside the interval. The corrected estimate is 3.3 points high. The judge's raw pass rate, 0.760, was 1.0 point low.

## 8. When the correction helps

Section 7 is one run. I ran the same calculation on all four v4 agent runs. After the freeze, I also measured the step 0 and step 2 judges on the same test split and v4 runs, as a secondary analysis. These runs were recorded as post-hoc in their manifests and changed nothing about the frozen judge.

| Judge | Test TPR | Test TNR | Agent config | Raw error | Corrected error | Ticket-level 95% CI contains the truth |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| step 0 (Jev) | 0.792 | 0.532 | clean | 3.5 | 23.0 | no |
| | | | template_edit | 8.5 | 26.0 | no |
| | | | context_strip | 7.0 | 10.5 | yes |
| | | | prompt_edit | 2.5 | 7.3 | yes |
| step 2 (Jev) | 0.906 | 0.774 | clean | 5.0 | 4.4 | yes |
| | | | template_edit | 4.5 | 5.0 | yes |
| | | | context_strip | 5.5 | 6.3 | yes |
| | | | prompt_edit | 2.0 | 3.7 | yes |
| step 3, frozen (Claude) | 0.927 | 0.919 | clean | 1.0 | 3.3 | yes |
| | | | template_edit | 1.0 | 2.7 | yes |
| | | | context_strip | 1.5 | 2.2 | yes |
| | | | prompt_edit | 0.5 | 2.4 | yes |

Errors are distance from the true pass rate in points. True pass rates of the four runs: 77.0%, 74.0%, 74.5% and 69.0%.

The correction was closer to the truth than the raw rate in 1 of 12 cases. For the step 0 judge it was badly wrong: it said every decision in two runs was correct, with intervals that excluded the truth.

The answer key shows why. The correction assumes the judge's TPR and TNR on each new run equal those measured on test. With the labels, they can be checked:

| Judge | Test TNR | Actual TNR on the four runs (clean, template_edit, context_strip, prompt_edit) |
|---|---|---|
| step 0 | 0.532 | 0.217, 0.192, 0.667, 0.419 |
| step 2 | 0.774 | 0.739, 0.769, 0.784, 0.790 |
| step 3, frozen | 0.919 | 0.935, 0.923, 0.961, 0.935 |

The step 0 judge misses some kinds of mistakes and catches others. Which mistakes a run contains depends on the agent's config, so the judge's TNR moves with it. A single test TNR averages over a mix that no particular run has. The frozen judge's rates are stable, but its test TPR (0.927) was a few points below its actual TPR on the v4 runs (0.96 to 0.97). With 96 passing test items that is within sampling error, and it was enough to push every corrected estimate up by 2 to 3 points.

So in this study the correction did not improve the point estimate for any judge. What it did provide, for the step 2 and step 3 judges, was an interval that contained the truth every time. For a good judge with balanced errors, the raw pass rate was already close. The correction cannot rescue a weak judge, because a weak judge's error rates do not carry over from one set of traces to the next. The order that matters is the one the method already gives: climb first, correct second.

## 9. What the answer key showed about the method

**9.1 Failures you construct are easier than failures that happen.** Before building the labeled set from agent decisions, I tried a cheaper one: every v2 ticket paired with every action, three wrong actions per ticket. On those items the step 0 judge had TNR 0.92. On the 12 wrong actions the agent had actually taken on the same tickets, its TNR was 0.17 (`paper/preliminary.md`). The judge rejects wrong answers the agent would never give and passes the ones it does give. A TNR measured on constructed failures would have made the judge look fine.

**9.2 A judge on the same model as the agent shares its blind spots.** The step 0 to step 2 judges and the agent are all Jev. The agent's most common mistakes on dev are refunds where the policy requires escalation (24 of 71) and reships or refunds where it requires only a reply (34), and these are the ones the Jev judges kept passing. Moving the same prompt to a different model removed most of them.

**9.3 The correction needs a good judge.** On paper 2's own data, the step 0 judge had TPR 0.87 and TNR 0.18, so TPR + TNR − 1 was 0.05 (`phase0/RESULTS.md`). Measured on half the tickets and applied to the other half over 2,000 random splits, the correction was undefined in 33.5% of splits. Where it was defined, its median error was 19.3 points, against 4.7 for the raw rate.

**9.4 Items that share a ticket are not independent.** Paper 2's 600 judged items were 60 tickets times 10 runs. Over 200 random half splits where the correction was defined (128 of them), judgy's 95% interval, which resamples items and holds p_obs fixed, contained the true rate 44% of the time. An interval that resamples tickets on both sides contained it 96% of the time. It was also about 100 points wide, which is the honest answer for that judge.

**9.5 Repeat agreement is not accuracy.** The step 0 judge's two calls agreed on 96.5% of items while it was wrong on a quarter of them. The frozen judge's calls agreed on 100%. Agreement says nothing about which of the two is right.

## 10. Limitations

- **One domain and one policy.** The thresholds, the number of steps and the size of each gain are specific to this task.
- **Generated tickets.** v3 and v4 come from phrase banks and read as more formulaic than real tickets. Their labels come from the policy function, so the wording does not affect correctness, but it may make the judge's job easier or harder than real traffic would.
- **The answer key is my reading of the policy.** Two cases are ambiguous under the policy text (Section 5). The labels were fixed before any judge was built and were not changed.
- **I wrote the few-shot critiques.** In the method a domain expert writes them. Here that was me, which is consistent with the method but is one person's wording.
- **Small labeled sets.** 158 items per split puts about ±5 points of sampling error on each rate, and Section 8 shows that this alone moves the corrected estimate by a few points.
- **The correction's point estimate was not helpful here.** The judges' errors were either balanced (step 3) or unstable across runs (step 0). A judge with stable, lopsided errors is the case the correction is built for, and this study does not contain one.
- **Model versions.** Jev was called through the alias `jev-latest`, which can point to a different model later. Claude was pinned to a dated ID.

## 11. Reproducibility

Everything is in [bfalkowski/judge-tpr-tnr](https://github.com/bfalkowski/judge-tpr-tnr): the ticket generator, the labeled set and splits, every judge version (`judge/judges.py`), the runners, the analysis scripts and the CI workflows. Every run, with its manifest and per-item verdicts, is on the `data` branch.

```
python analysis/climb.py     # the climb table
python analysis/final.py     # test, correction and post-hoc tables
python analysis/phase0.py    # the paper 2 judge on paper 2's data
```

Recorded API spend was $1.78. A further dev run of about $0.57 was discarded before its results were saved, because of a bug in the workflow's secret check.

**How this was made.** I designed the study, chose the method and the decisions recorded before the test run, and reviewed the results. I worked with Claude in the Claude app on October 7 to 11, 2026: it wrote most of the code and drafts of the text with me and ran the analysis, which I checked against the raw runs. The session was configured for model ID `claude-opus-5-5`; the service can route individual turns to a different model. The judge in step 3 is a separate model, Claude Haiku 4.5, called through the API.

Not affiliated with TypeSafe, Anthropic or Parlance Labs.
